THIEVING COPS 2015

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Criminal Cops caught on camera moving R3 million stolen clothing in police cars.

Summary:
WE HAVE EXCLUSIVE CCTV FOOTAGE SHOW A GANG OF COPS FROM LANGLAAGTE MOVING STOLEN GOODS OFF A TRUCK THEY JUST HIJACKED – IN UNIFORM AND USING POLICE CARS.

According to this year’s crime stats, truck hijacking jumped 29 percent to 1279 incidents – that’s at least three a day with billions of rands in losses.

We ask if the spike in truck hijackings could be because the police that are meant to investigate these crimes are actually the criminals doing the hijacking!

Further information:
From petrol tankers to food to clothing – if it’s a commodity that can be moved it will be stolen! But criminal syndicates have the upper hand with cops not only protecting them but in this case committing the actual crime. We've done truck hijacking stories - now we look specifically at the trend of police involvement and how it is linked to the increase in this type of crime.

On the 28th of October a truck carrying R6million of branded clothing was pulled over in a police roadblock on the N1. But the four policemen in uniform using police vehicles were on unofficial business – it was truck hijacking. The driver was taken hostage, and dumped a few kilometers down the road. The cops escourted the truck to a plot in Crown Mines where they proceded to move the boxes of clothing using their police cars to a different location. Police tracking systems confirm that the two vehicles are from the Langlaagte Police station and that they moved between the plot in Crown Mines to a location just five kilometers away.

This is all captured on CCTV footage. You can clearly see one policeman holding watch, patrolling up and down the street while two marked police cars transport the goods. The police captian in charge of the shift that night also makes an appearance on the scene, interacts with the cop-jackets and then drives off.

Initially no arrests were made, there were only talks of a possible warning being issued. Eventually two days later after threatening to go to Carte Blanche were four of the five cops arrested. The shift captain is still on duty and has not been arrested.

No statements were taken from witnesses who saw the cops transporting the goods. An ID parade was held but the driver of the hijacked truck was not called.

We speak to an insider who specialises in truck-hijacking investigations with over 25 years experience – he has seen the spike in this crime linked to more and more cases where cops are involved, yet there is a clear reluctance on the part of the police to arrest their own despite often having damning evidence.

The Road Freight Association has statistics available to help quantify the losses.

Press Release:


Thieving Cops
Several Johannesburg-based police officers linked to a truck-hijacking syndicate, thought they would get away with setting out in police vehicles and in uniform, to steal designer clothing worth millions. The officers proceeded to offload the bounty, but in their haste, neglected to notice the CCTV cameras filming their every move. Could this year’s 29% spike in truck hijackings be related in part to
cops - who are meant to investigate these crimes - actually perpetrating them? Carte Blanche’s exclusive footage helps bring corrupt cops to book.


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Corrupt cops have been the subject many Carte Blanche investigations.

In 2012, Cop-jackers were caught on camera in police gear using marked vehicles to hijack civilians.

In 2014, we exposed a member of the Brixton Flying Squad that hi-jacked a truck carrying R500 000 in fuel.

This year truck-jackings are up by 29 %. That’s 24 trucks a week - costing the economy a devastating R100 billion in losses every year.

Industry insiders say it’s because more often than not, cops are the criminals behind truck-juckings.

INSIDER: // the police are now being paid just to pull off the vehicle, R50 000 for the pull off, and when they stage a roadblock every police man will be paid between R20 and R25 000 depending on the value of the load. INT 1 M6 –

VO: It’s money well spent for criminals, because it buys them protection. A trend HAWKS Spokesperson Brigadier Mulaudzi acknowledges.

BONGANI: If officers are involved, it gives criminals a sense of confidence?
BRIGADIER: Obviously, they are working with people of authority, they are working with people who give them information.

VO: And sometimes cops even offer add-on services – like transporting stolen goods.

This exclusive CCTV footage shows thieves loading stolen goods off a hijacked truck, into marked police vehicles. The cops brazenly moved load after load in broad daylight, while one officer keeps watch on the road – walking up and down keeping an eye out.

Truck hijacking is a high-stakes business after all!

LINK: It could be anything from electronics to something as simple as baby formula, if it can be sold, it will be stolen.

VO: Unlike regular vehicle hijacking, this is a highly sophisticated crime that yields big profits says Gareth Newham from the Institute for Security Studies.

Gareth: When you hijacking a truck, you’ve gotta have quite an organised network to get rid of all the goods, you’ve gotta be able to hide the truck, transport the goods, so it’s a much bigger operation.




VO: Commodities that can be sold quickly on the black market are prime targets.

Driver Joseph, was transporting R6 million in branded clothing when he was pulled over at an apparent road block on the N1 close to Sebokeng.

JOSEPH: Since I saw the police cars standing here, I just relax and say to myself there is nothing here.

VO: And when a uniformed policeman asked to see his license, he still wasn’t suspicious.

JOSEPH: I tried to give him my license, he pulled the door, he jumped very fast and hit me with the gun on my head. And he said lie on your bed, just don’t look at me.

VO: Joseph was caught off guard and feared for his life.

JOSEPH: I was praying to God that he may give me strength that I will go out there still alive. Because he was busy telling me it was last day, I must pray.

VO: But a quick get-away was the main priority. Joseph was left on the side of the high way as the truck drove off with the prized cargo.

It arrived at Crowne Mines, an industrial area south of Johannesburg around 23.30 that night – from here on out their every move would be captured on camera.

First the hijacked trucked pulled into the plot. Then a second truck arrived a while later parking outside. This truck was meant to move the stolen goods – but it broke down as trucks do.

But all was not lost, this is when the criminals got innovative. They called in the emergency services of two branded police cars. In a space of 5 hours, they did eight trips, making off with R3 million in stolen branded clothing.

LINK: It’s almost hard to believe, the vans in the footage, are actual police vehicles, the uniformed personnel, are real policeman from Langlaagte Police Station.

GARETH: When the police are willing to commit crimes on duty in uniform in public suggests that they really do not for a second think that they will be held accountable.

VO: Around 06.30 the next morning the cops were caught red-handed by the transporter’s tracking company.

LINK: What’s really even more incredible to believe is the fact that despite the clear evidence of wrongdoing, they weren’t immediately charged or arrested.

VO: Only the Driver of the second truck and mechanic on the plot were arrested on the scene.

Despite numerous senior officials having looked at the footage, it was decided that there was not enough evidence to arrest the cops.

INSIDER: He said that he will just warn the guys that they must not interfere with any of the witnesses, and that they must, when they get to a scene, report to their commander immediately when they find any stolen goods.

VO: It was only when they were threatened with Carte Blanche that the decision was reconsidered.

INSIDER: Only then did he compromise and say that it’s actually a strong case and issued an instruction for the guys to be arrested immediately.

VO: This reluctance to take action, is in itself criminal says Gareth.

GARETH: If those commanders are not taking the appropriate criminal and disciplinary action as a matter of urgency, they themselves are threat to the public support for the SA police service.

VO: Brigadier Mulaudzi was disturbed by these allegations.

BRIGADIER: It is wrong. It is wrong. And I think it is critical that when we do our own investigation from an anti-corruption point of view, // whether you are a brigadier or colonel, if you involve yourself in trying to cover up, you know for a fact that it’s defeating the ends of justice.

VO: Four cops were eventually arrested and are currently out on R3000 bail.

A fifth cop has been implicated - a Captain Sibanda, who was in charge of the uniformed officers. He was allegedly on the scene driving this unmarked police Ford Icon.

He was at the scene for around 10 minutes. He watched as one of the police vans was loaded and then watched it race off. A third police car, that arrived with Captain Sibanda, reversed into the plot, possibly to take another load. But the tracking company arrived and stopped them in their tracks.

INSIDER: when he was questioned about his presence at the scene, he first said that he couldn’t remember that he was there but // it was confirmed that the vehicle was booked out to him and we showed him on the footage that he was at the scene, he just said that his members alerted him concerning a truck hijacking and therefore for that reason he went out to the scene.

VO: We called Captain Sibanda.

Bongani: You can’t tell us why you were there?
CAPt Sibanda: Call the, call the communications he will come with you.
Bongani: you cant remember if you were there or not?
CAPt Sibanda: Ja, I can’t remember.
Bongani: We’ve got footage that places you there, we know you were there, you know you were there. What were you doing there?
CAPt Sibanda: There’s no comment, there’s no comment.
BONGANI: But what were you doing there?
CAPT SIBANDA: I can’t cimment.
BONGANI: Are you involved with police corruption?
CALL CUTS OUT

VO: Just the allegation is a serious concern to start with according to Gareth.

GARETH: when a captain or a commissioning officer is implicated or there is any allegation of a crime, then you are talking about a much bigger network and much more dangerous network of people that needs to be dealt with.

VO: We put the allegations to Brigadier Mulaudzi.

BONGANI: With Respect – more than a month – not arrested…
BRIgADIER:
BONGANI: Can we agree that if syndicates are hijacking trucks, it’s organised crime?
BRIGADIER: yes
BONGANI: Can we agree that if officers are involved in this it is organised crime?
BRIGADIER: Correct
BONGANI: So what have you done about it?
BRIGADIER: We are acting with urgency…
CUT
BONGANI: Are the four that have been arrested still at work?
BRIGADIER: They have been served internally
BONGANI: so only now, almost a month later // could they possibly be suspended
BRIGADIER: It is true, that is true, I think we will have to check as to what has transpired for them to take so long to come to that decision. INT 1 M25

VO: Richard fears that the investigation may be at risk with the cops still on active duty.

INSIDER: This case has been assigned to three different investigating officers, apart from the initial investigation and the witness statements that were obtained there was absolutely nothing further investigation done on this matter.

VO: We headed out to the scene in Crown Mines.

LINK: This is the plot where the hijacked truck was recovered and the stolen goods moved. Let’s find out who the plot belongs to and why the truck was here?

Bongani: hello!
Bongani: Who owns this place?
DRIVER: Hassan.

VO: We had a quick look around, the trucks inside weren’t operational, apparently, Hassan’s transport business closed down after he too was a victim of truck-hijacking. We were given a contact number for him.

BONGANI: How were the suspects linked to your property?
HASSAN: The guy there, the mechanic he was also arrested, I think he is involved in it.

VO: Nervous about any possible retaliation, Hassan didn’t want to comment further as he was aware of the police involvement.

Gareth believes the current situation with criminal cops is because of a profound failure of leadership.

Gareth: The most senior South African police service officials for too long have completely disregarded their own code of conduct and that is now filtering down the organisation and it’s providing ample space for police officials to start joining criminal gangs because it’s so lucrative and the chance of being held accountable is so unlikely.

VO: But Brigadier Mulaudzi is confident that criminal cops, be they constables or brigadier, will be brought to book.

BRIGADIER: We want to warn them that we are looking at you, and you can run, but you can’t hide – we will come after you – irrespective of who you are.

VO: But while corruption rules, people like Joseph remain very skeptical of the police.

JOSEPH: I know there are good police, there are bad police, but you can’t even differentiate.

PROMO 1
VO: Could 2015’s 29% spike in truck hijackings be because cops are the criminals behind the crime?

JOSEPH: I know there are good police, there are bad police, but you can’t even differentiate.

PROMO 2
VO: Criminal Cops caught on camera brazenly moving R3 million in stolen clothing in police cars.

GARETH: When the police are willing to commit crimes on duty in uniform in public suggests that they really do not for a second think that they will be held accountable.

PROMO 3

VO: Thieving cops make off with R3 million in stolen clothing – their every move caught on camera.

BRIGADIER: You know it’s very disturbing, embarrassing as well, for me to listen to such kind of allegations

VO: We bring you exclusive footage exposing these cops.

According to this year’s crime stats, truck hijacking jumped 29 percent to 1279 incidents – that’s at least three a day with billions of rands in losses. We ask if the spike in truck hijackings could be because the police that are meant to investigate these crimes are actually the criminals doing the hijacking!
metadata.Further information: From petrol tankers to food to clothing – if it’s a commodity that can be moved it will be stolen! But criminal syndicates have the upper hand with cops not only protecting them but in this case committing the actual crime. We've done truck hijacking stories - now we look specifically at the trend of police involvement and how it is linked to the increase in this type of crime. On the 28th of October a truck carrying R6million of branded clothing was pulled over in a police roadblock on the N1. But the four policemen in uniform using police vehicles were on unofficial business – it was truck hijacking. The driver was taken hostage, and dumped a few kilometers down the road. The cops escourted the truck to a plot in Crown Mines where they proceded to move the boxes of clothing using their police cars to a different location. Police tracking systems confirm that the two vehicles are from the Langlaagte Police station and that they moved between the plot in Crown Mines to a location just five kilometers away. This is all captured on CCTV footage. You can clearly see one policeman holding watch, patrolling up and down the street while two marked police cars transport the goods. The police captian in charge of the shift that night also makes an appearance on the scene, interacts with the cop-jackets and then drives off. Initially no arrests were made, there were only talks of a possible warning being issued. Eventually two days later after threatening to go to Carte Blanche were four of the five cops arrested. The shift captain is still on duty and has not been arrested. No statements were taken from witnesses who saw the cops transporting the goods. An ID parade was held but the driver of the hijacked truck was not called. We speak to an insider who specialises in truck-hijacking investigations with over 25 years experience – he has seen the spike in this crime linked to more and more cases where cops are involved, yet there is a clear reluctance on the part of the police to arrest their own despite often having damning evidence. The Road Freight Association has statistics available to help quantify the losses.
